comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Baseline landed (sized-grid-amf), so this is now measurable rather than speculative.

The strongest single number: 'tabulate' on a 300x300 grid of Int allocates 93 MB and
takes 23.6 ms. The payload of that grid is 90,000 boxed Ints, well under 1 MB. Roughly
1 KB of allocation per cell is exactly the someNatVal / KnownNat-dictionary traffic this
issue describes -- every Ordinal construction builds a type-level natural.

Supporting figures, all GHC 9.12.3 aarch64-darwin -O1:
    index x90000, 300x300      13.8 ms,  72 MB   (153 ns and ~800 B per index)
    ifoldl' 300x300            19.5 ms, 107 MB
    extend neighbourSum 50x50  5.42 ms,  29 MB   (2.2 us per cell, 9 peeks each)
    (.+^) Periodic             157 ns/op, 1.1 KB/op
    toEnum/fromEnum HardWrap    24 ns/op

Compare 'fmap 300x300' at 758 us / 4.1 MB, which touches every cell but constructs no
Ordinals. That is the target the newtype-over-Int representation should be aiming at.

Re-run 'cabal run bench:benchmarks' and diff against
bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv to judge the refactor.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Done in commit "Make Ordinal a newtype over Int" (branch worktree-ordinal-int).

Shipped as proposed: newtype over Int with a nominal role, constructor not
exported, numToOrdinal as the checked entry point and unsafeOrdinal as the one
unchecked one (assert-guarded). asSizeProxy's evidence is rebuilt on demand by
reifyOrdinal at the single call site (shrinkGrid) instead of being carried in
every value. Signatures that gained a constraint the GADT used to smuggle in:
asSizeProxy (KnownNat n), ShrinkableGrid (KnownNat x), maxCoord (1 <= n).

Result, A/B measured in one session:

    (.+^) Periodic 300x300      2.07x faster, 49% less allocated
    toEnum/fromEnum HardWrap    2.50x faster, 61% less allocated
    extend neighbourSum         1.12x faster, 11% less allocated
    (.-.) HardWrap              1.22x faster,  5% less allocated
    tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl' unchanged to within 1%

The estimate in this issue's earlier comment -- that tabulate's 93 MB was
someNatVal/KnownNat traffic -- was wrong, and the benchmark says so plainly.
allCoord shares 600 Ordinals across 90,000 coords, so per-value representation
never dominated the grid-wide operations. The remaining cost is NP allocation
plus coordPosition's Integer arithmetic; both belong to sized-grid-uvd, which
now has the numbers on it.

Also note the measurement trap hit on the way: the recorded baseline CSV was
1.9x off because the machine was busier than when it was written, which made a
2x win read as a 2x regression. bench/Main.hs now documents measuring both
sides in one session.

title: allCoord is rebuilt from scratch on every imap/ifoldMap/itraverse/tabulate
description:
src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:67-75

    imap func (Grid v)      = Grid $ V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v
    ifoldMap func (Grid v)  = foldMap id $ V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v
    itraverse func (Grid v) = Grid <$> sequenceA (V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v)

and src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:64

    tabulate func = Grid $ V.fromList $ map func allCoord

'allCoord' (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:206-212) builds the full coordinate list through
the list monad over an NP, then V.fromList copies it into a vector. This happens on
every single indexed traversal, and each element is a heap-allocated NP I cs whose
components each carry a KnownNat dictionary.

For Grid '[HardWrap 300, HardWrap 300] that is 90,000 NP allocations per imap.

Also src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:220-237: coordPosition recomputes the per-axis size
product ('sizeOfList') on every call, in Integer, and index calls coordPosition for
every access.

Options, roughly in order of payoff:
  1. Cache the coordinate vector per type in a CAF: 'allCoordVector :: V.Vector (Coord cs)'
     bound at top level so GHC shares it across calls. Needs care to actually float.
  2. Precompute the axis strides once (a small [Int]) rather than folding sizes each
     time in coordPosition.
  3. Better: make imap/ifoldMap/itraverse iterate positions as Int and only
     materialise a Coord when the user function demands one. Most callers use
     fromEnum on the result anyway -- see ../aoc/src/2018/11.hs:40
     '(fromEnum -> r) :| (fromEnum -> c) :| _'.

Depends on the Ordinal representation change for the biggest win.
close_reason: Fixed on branch worktree-allcoord. coordPosition is a single Int pass (was Integer with a per-axis re-traversal); tabulate uses V.fromListN coordSpaceSize; ifoldr/ifoldl' given outright. allCoord itself was not the problem - the V.fromList in the traversals fuses. 24-49% less allocation across tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl'/extend, 110 tests pass, zero warnings. Remainder tracked as sized-grid-0vl.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Quantified by sized-grid-amf's baseline (GHC 9.12.3, aarch64-darwin, -O1). The
benchmark pairs each allCoord-using operation with the closest operation that does not
use it, so the difference is attributable:

    tabulate 300x300  23.6 ms,  93 MB   vs   pure 300x300  206 us, 704 KB   -> 115x, 132x alloc
    imap     300x300  17.7 ms,  80 MB   vs   fmap 300x300  758 us, 4.1 MB   ->  23x,  20x alloc

allCoord is not overhead on indexed traversal, it is essentially the entire cost. Re-run
'cabal run bench:benchmarks' after any caching change and compare against
bench/baseline-ghc9.12.3-aarch64-darwin.csv.

Note there is no standalone allCoord benchmark and it is not an oversight: at a fixed
type allCoord is a CAF and the optimiser shares it, so a direct measurement reports ~2 ns
for 90,000 coordinates. Details in the comment in bench/Main.hs.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Measured correction from the sized-grid-upo work (commit "Make Ordinal a newtype
over Int"). The Ordinal representation is NOT what tabulate/imap/index/ifoldl'
are paying for. A/B with both sides measured in one session:

    (.+^) Periodic          2.07x faster, 49% less allocated
    toEnum/fromEnum         2.50x faster, 61% less allocated
    tabulate 300x300        unchanged: 97,580,033 -> 97,421,177 bytes
    imap 300x300            unchanged: 83,502,208 -> 83,502,303 bytes
    index x90000            unchanged: 75,581,477 -> 75,581,480 bytes
    ifoldl' 300x300         unchanged: 112,040,243 -> 111,881,769 bytes

Why: allCoord is a cartesian product over the per-axis lists, so for a 300x300
grid it constructs 600 Ordinals and shares them across all 90,000 NPs. Ordinal
construction was never the per-cell cost. What is left, and what this issue now
owns in full, is:

  1. the 90,000 NP I cs allocations themselves, rebuilt per traversal, and
  2. coordPosition, which is called per cell and does its arithmetic in Integer
     -- ordinalToNum boxes an Integer per axis, and sizeOfList recomputes the
     stride product per call.

(2) is now a clean win to take: ordinalToInt gives the axis value as an Int
directly, so coordPosition can be Int throughout with the strides precomputed
once. That did not exist before the newtype.

Judge any change here by the allocation columns, not the times -- see the note
added to bench/Main.hs about cross-session drift.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
Done. The issue's premise was wrong in an instructive way, so the result is recorded here in full.

allCoord is NOT rebuilt in the sense meant. 'V.zipWith func (V.fromList allCoord) v' fuses: the coordinates are produced and consumed one at a time and never all exist at once. Its real cost is about 67 bytes a cell. I confirmed this by breaking it -- building the coordinate vector from a recursive function, and separately by putting the same list under V.fromListN -- and both made imap 23% more allocation and 59% slower, with ifoldl' copying jumping from 48KB to 18MB. The fused form is now commented as such in SizedGrid.Grid.Grid so it does not get "fixed" again.

What the benchmark gap actually measured was coordPosition, which tabulate/imap/ifoldl' are all handed as their per-cell function: ~800 bytes per call. The old version recomputed the axis-size product with a separate traversal per axis, in Integer.

Changes:
  - coordPosition is one Int pass; the stride of an axis is the size of the axes below it, which comes back up the recursion.
  - tabulate uses V.fromListN coordSpaceSize (its result is a vector regardless, so the exact length just avoids growth doubling).
  - ifoldr/ifoldl' given outright rather than derived from ifoldMap through an Endo chain.
  - New API: coordSpaceSize (MaxCoordSize as a value, needing only All IsCoordLifted) and coordFromPosition (checked inverse of coordPosition).
  - 10 new tests pinning the position/coordinate bijection and that imap/ifoldMap/ifoldr/ifoldl' agree with tabulate and with each other. Mutation-checked: a wrong stride fails 6 of them.

Allocated, before -> after (the deterministic column):
  tabulate 300x300    97,421,177 ->  73,740,888   -24%
  imap 300x300        83,502,303 ->  62,641,438   -25%
  index x90000        75,581,480 ->  54,720,335   -28%
  ifoldl' 300x300    111,881,769 ->  57,600,340   -49%
  extend 50x50        27,045,702 ->  21,808,586   -19%
  extract 50x50              808 ->         608   -25%
  itraverse 100x100   unchanged; everything else unchanged

Times, both sides measured in one session:
  tabulate 47.0ms -> 33.4ms, imap 33.9 -> 22.8, index 27.0 -> 15.0,
  ifoldl' 38.0 -> 15.1, extend 9.39ms -> 6.23ms, extract 298ns -> 167ns

Baseline CSV re-recorded. The "allCoord overhead" benchmark group is renamed to "indexed vs unindexed (the gap is coordPosition, not allCoord)" -- its old name and its pairing are what pointed this issue at the wrong thing.

What is left is sized-grid-0vl: coordPosition's remaining ~550 bytes a call is dictionary plumbing (peeling IsCoordLifted out of All, natVal boxing an Integer, the Iso call for asOrdinal), not arithmetic.

title: takeGrid and splitHigherDim have unsound type signatures (no n <= m; z unconstrained)
description:
CONFIRMED empirically.

1) takeGrid -- src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:197-198

    takeGrid :: KnownNat n => Proxy n -> Grid '[c m] x -> Grid '[c n] x
    takeGrid p (Grid v) = Grid $ V.take (fromIntegral $ natVal p) v

Missing 'n <= m'. Probe:
    takeGrid (Proxy @9) (gridFromList [1,2,3] :: Grid '[Ordinal 3] Int) :: Grid '[Ordinal 9] Int
    => unGrid length 3, while the type claims 9. Invariant broken, silently.

2) splitHigherDim -- src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:200-219

    splitHigherDim :: forall c as x y z a. (KnownNat x, KnownNat y, y <= x, ...)
      => Grid (c x ': as) a -> (Grid (c y ': as) a, Grid (c z ': as) a)

'z' is a completely free type variable in the result. The caller picks any z they
like and the second component's type is a lie unless they happen to pick x - y.
tests/Main.hs:136-138 only passes because it annotates z correctly by hand.

3) dropGrid -- src/SizedGrid/Grid/Grid.hs:190-195 has the same shape of problem;
   'm - n' is stuck rather than checked when n > m.

Fix: add 'n <= m' to takeGrid/dropGrid and fix splitHigherDim's result to
'Grid (c (x - y) ': as) a'. This is a breaking API change but restores the
core guarantee the library exists to provide.

Related: this class of hole is exactly what ghc-typelits-natnormalise +
ghc-typelits-knownnat make cheap to state and discharge.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
FIXED. takeGrid and dropGrid now require 'n <= m'; splitHigherDim's remainder is 'c (x - y)' instead of a free variable.

The stricter signatures immediately caught a fourth bug: ShrinkableGrid's window constraint had x and y transposed. Filed and fixed as sized-grid-px9.

Consequence for the tests: the two cases that used to fail at RUNTIME are now compile errors ('Cannot satisfy: 9 <= 3'), so they cannot be runtime assertions any more. They are documented in tests/Test/Invariant.hs and a compile-fail harness is filed as sized-grid-cti. The positive half (sizes promised == sizes held) is still asserted.

No impact on ../aoc: it uses none of takeGrid/dropGrid/splitHigherDim/shrinkGrid.

title: axisSteps rescans its candidate list per candidate: the real neighbourhood cost, 67% of it
description:
sized-grid-5uq moved the stepsWithin fold into an IsCoordList method, which is
correct and unrolls, and it was worth 9% of the allocation. The remaining cost
is one function below it, in axisSteps, and it is most of the benchmark.

MEASURED, both sides in one session, on 'extend neighbourSum 50x50':

  HEAD before 5uq                      6.84 ms / 25.71 MB
  after 5uq (the fold as a method)     6.46 ms / 23.42 MB
  with the dedup scan skipped          2.24 ms / 12 MB     (67% less than HEAD)

So the fold was ~9% and this is the rest.

WHAT IT IS. axisSteps builds 'reachable' and then, per element, scans that whole
list again with 'any (beats (d, v)) reachable' --- quadratic in the number of
candidates, with a closure allocated per element. The scan exists to drop
duplicates: on a torus axis with 2*r >= n two offsets reach the same value, and
the one that took fewer steps has to win so that the recorded distance is the
true distance.

THE EXPERIMENT that produced the 2.24 ms was a guard skipping the scan when it
cannot fire:

    axisSteps r c
        | 2 * r + 1 <= ordinalSize @(CoordNat x) = [(abs d, v) | (d, v) <- reachable]
        | otherwise = <the scan as it is now>

Sound for the library's own axes. On a bounded axis the surviving values are at
position i + d and so are distinct for distinct d whatever r is; on Periodic
they are (i + d) mod n, distinct exactly when 2*r + 1 <= n. When every key is
distinct no element beats another --- 'beats' requires key equality, and an
element never beats itself --- so the fast path is elementwise equal to the
scan, order included.

THE DECISION TO MAKE, and why this was not landed with 5uq. The argument above
is about what offsetIsCoord does, not about what the class promises. A
third-party IsCoord with a reflecting boundary --- offset +1 from the top edge
coming back to n-2 --- would satisfy the stated law relating offsetIsCoord to
(.+^) and still produce duplicates under the guard. Either the guard is right
and IsCoord should say that offsetIsCoord is injective in d where it is Just,
or the dedup has to stay unconditional and get cheaper another way (scan the
candidates in (abs d, d) order keeping the first per key, which is the same
answer without the per-element rescan). That is a call about the class contract,
so it is filed rather than assumed.

VERIFY WITH 'extend neighbourSum 50x50' in bench/Main.hs, measuring both sides
now per that file's header. Do not read against the recorded CSV. The 334 tests
in tests/Test/Neighbours.hs already cover the torus cases the scan is for ---
'vonNeumannNeighbours 2' on a 3-cycle, 'mooreNeighbours 2' on a 4-torus --- so
they are the check on whatever replaces it.
notes:
RESOLVED BY MEASUREMENT, NOT BY THE DECISION THIS ISSUE ASKED FOR.

The premise was wrong. The cost was not the quadratic dedup scan; it was that
axisSteps is out of line and so folds nothing it calls. One INLINE pragma:

  extend neighbourSum 50x50   6.51 ms / 22 MB  ->  2.12 ms / 9.9 MB  (67% less)

Every other benchmark in the suite unmoved, measured both sides in one session.
All 334 tests plus the downstream and readme suites pass.

WHY THE SCAN WAS NOT THE CAUSE. The neighbourhood functions run at r = 1, so
reachable has three elements and the scan is nine comparisons. Out of line each
one paid a dictionary. Before-Core of $waxisSteps:

  offsetIsCoord $dIsCoord $dKnownNat irred (eta `cast` ...) ds

per candidate, boxing a fresh ds = I# x1, and per inner element of the scan:

  asOrdinal $dIsCoord $fProfunctorFUN $fFunctorConst (lvl10 `cast` ...) (v' `cast` ...)

After-Core at '[Clamped 50, Clamped 50]: reachable is a go loop over Int# whose
body is ># x (-# 49# y) and <# x (negateInt# y), the bounds check against a
literal with no Natural anywhere; the scan is a joinrec, so no closure per
element; key is case v `cast` ... of I# x, asOrdinal reduced to a coercion; and
the (abs d', d') < (abs d, d) tuple comparison is branches on Int# with no
tuples built. No axisSteps, offsetIsCoord, npStepsWithin, integerFromNatural or
dictionary argument survives in the benchmark's Core.

THE CONTRACT DECISION IS DECLINED, and does not need making. The guard measured
2.24 ms / 12 MB -- slower than the INLINE -- so the injectivity law would have
bought nothing. It would also have cost: a reflecting boundary reaches the same
value from +d and -d at an edge, satisfies every law IsCoord currently states,
and is precisely what the fork's thesis (the coordinate type is the boundary
policy, sized-grid-85n) exists to admit. Narrowing the class to buy speed the
compiler gives away for free is the wrong trade.

Commit 66d50ee. Doc note added at axisSteps; the stale claim in the
offsetByPosition note that the residue was the fold above it is corrected.
close_reason: Closed

title: offsetByPosition reads its KnownNat as a run-time Natural on every call
description:
The per-axis step of the checked offset, below the fold sized-grid-135 fixed.

With npOffset in place the axis-list fold unrolls and the remaining cost is all
in the step. From the Core of SizedGrid.Coord.Class at -O1:

    $woffsetByPosition
      = \ @c @n $dIsCoord $dKnownNat c1 ww ->
          case integerToInt# (integerFromNatural ($dKnownNat `cast` ...)) of ds
          { __DEFAULT ->
          case (asOrdinal $dIsCoord $fProfunctorFUN $fFunctorConst ... c1) ...

Two things per call, per axis:
  1. the axis size is recovered from a run-time Natural --- integerFromNatural
     then integerToInt# --- rather than being the literal it is at a concrete
     axis. At the call site the dictionary is 'main81 = NS 300##', so the 300 is
     right there and never folded.
  2. asOrdinal is called through the lens dictionaries ($fProfunctorFUN,
     $fFunctorConst) rather than as the coercion it is.

Compare the (.+^) path on the same shape, which folds the size to a literal:
coordPosition at '[Clamped 300, Clamped 300] is '+# (*# x3 300#) x4'.

EVIDENCE. 'offsetCoord x360000, checked, over Clamped 300x300' in bench/Main.hs
is 199 MB and 57.0 ms after sized-grid-135 (268 MB / 73.0 ms before it), against
66 bytes and 1.92 ms for 'cornerReads', which is the same 360,000 offsets over
the same coords through (.+^). Roughly 550 bytes per checked offset, and the
fold is no longer any of it.

APPROACH, unproven, measure before committing to it. offsetIsCoord's default is
offsetByPosition and the size arrives as KnownNat n on the method rather than
through the instance, so specialisation has no concrete n to fix. Worth trying:
INLINE on the default, or ordinalSize taking the size some way that constant
folds. Note that -fspecialise-aggressively did not rescue the analogous case in
sized-grid-czf, so do not assume a flag will do it.

Affects offsetCoord, offsetCoordUpTo and coordRay, which all bottom out here,
and axisSteps calls offsetIsCoord directly too --- so this is also part of the
neighbourhood cost tracked separately.
close_reason:
Fixed by a one-line INLINE on offsetByPosition (commit e53afc2, branch worktree-bw8-offsetbyposition-knownnat).

offsetCoord x360000, checked, over Clamped 300x300: 56.4 ms / 199 MB -> 6.85 ms / 35 MB. Full suite: 2 improve, 17 unchanged, no regressions. 334 tests, downstream and readme all pass.

THE DIAGNOSIS WAS RIGHT, both halves. Before, the per-axis call was an out-of-line $w$coffsetIsCoord main81 ds3 ww2 -- passing the NS 300## dictionary at run time. After, it is an inline ># x (-# 299# y1) per axis: the size folds to a literal, asOrdinal reduces to coercions instead of applications of $fProfunctorFUN and $fFunctorConst, and the Maybe becomes join points. Zero occurrences of offsetIsCoord remain in the whole benchmark's Core.

WHY INLINE WORKED HERE, given the issue warned it might not. The IsCoordList note establishes that INLINE cannot rescue a fold that is self-recursive and polymorphic in the axis list, and that -fspecialise-aggressively did not either. Neither applies: offsetByPosition is small and not recursive, and sized-grid-135 had already made the axis fold an instance method, so every per-axis call site already held a statically resolved KnownNat. The two results compose rather than conflict -- a class indexed by the axis list fixes the fold, inlining fixes the step the fold then calls directly. Worth remembering as the rule for the rest of this chain.

CHECK THE CORE FROM THE RIGHT ARTIFACT. The issue quoted $woffsetByPosition from the library's own dump, which shows the generic worker that exists for polymorphic callers and is not what a concrete call site runs. The claim only holds up read from the consumer's dump (bench/Main.dump-simpl). A stale library in a shared builddir also produced a misleading dump mid-session; the before/after was settled by building each side into its own builddir.

WHAT IS LEFT of the 35 MB is not the bounds check, which now allocates nothing -- it is the closure the benchmark's own comprehension builds per position.

FOUND ON THE WAY: sized-grid-xv4, the same run-time-Natural read still in axisBoundaryByPosition, the default axisDistanceIsCoord, and Periodic's offsetIsCoord override. Left alone deliberately: no benchmark reaches them, so the change could not be measured.

SIDE EFFECT WORTH RECORDING: extend neighbourSum 50x50 fell 8.88 ms / 28 MB -> 7.01 ms / 25 MB with the neighbourhood fold untouched, because axisSteps calls offsetIsCoord per candidate. sized-grid-5uq's recorded baseline has been updated; it was 9.02 ms / 28 MB and reading against that would now understate the fold.

title: stepsWithin folds the axis list with a helper that cannot unroll: the real neighbourhood cost
description:
Third instance of the defect sized-grid-czf and sized-grid-135 fixed, and this is the one the neighbourhood workloads actually run.

sized-grid-135 was filed on the premise that 'the neighbourhood path is what
gameOfLife, ising-example and ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs and 2018/18.hs actually run'
and that the path went through offsetCoord. It does not. neighbours =
mooreNeighbours 1, and mooreNeighbours r c = [n | (s, n) <- stepsWithin r c, s > 0].
stepsWithin never calls offsetCoord.

What it calls is its own where-helper (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs):

    stepsWithin r (Coord cs) = fmap Coord <$> go cs
      where
        go :: IsCoordList xs => NP I xs -> [(Int, NP I xs)]
        go Nil = [(0, Nil)]
        go (I x :* xs) = do
            (d, v) <- axisSteps r x
            (s, rest) <- go xs
            return (d + s, I v :* rest)

Self-recursive and polymorphic in the axis list, so it cannot unroll and every
axis after the first peels the IsCoordList dictionary at run time. Exactly the
shape of the two folds already moved into class methods.

EVIDENCE. 'extend neighbourSum 50x50' is 2,500 cells x 8 Moore neighbours. It
measured 9.17 ms / 28 MB before sized-grid-czf, 9.18 ms / 28 MB after it, and
9.02 ms / 28 MB after sized-grid-135. Neither fold fix touched it, because
neither fold is on this path. That is what identifies this helper.

APPROACH. Same as the other two: an IsCoordList method. The per-axis step is
axisSteps, whose only obligation is IsCoordLifted x, which IsCoordList already
supplies per axis -- so like npOffset and unlike AffineCoordList, this needs no
new class and is not a breaking change. Note the step also carries the radius r,
so the method takes it as an argument.

axisSteps is worth a look in the same pass but is a separate cost: it builds a
'reachable' list per axis per call and filters it with 'any' over that same
list, which is quadratic in r.

VERIFY WITH 'extend neighbourSum 50x50' in bench/Main.hs, measuring both sides
now per that file's header. Do not read against the recorded CSV.
notes:
DONE in 7915bff. The fold is now npStepsWithin, an IsCoordList method; axisSteps
moved to SizedGrid.Coord.Class so the method could be stated there, and
SizedGrid.Coord re-exports it, so no import changes and no breaking change ---
the approach in the issue was right that IsCoordList already supplies the
per-axis obligation.

Core verified at '[Clamped 50, Clamped 50]: the fold unrolls to two per-axis
loops calling $waxisSteps directly, no axis-list dictionary, no recursion left.

MEASURED, both sides in one session, 'extend neighbourSum 50x50':
  25,709,079 B / 6.840 ms  ->  23,421,527 B / 6.544 ms   (-8.9% alloc, -4.3%)
Every other benchmark's allocation byte-identical. 334 tests, downstream and
readme pass.

THE FINDING, which is worth more than the fix: the issue's premise was half
wrong. The fold was real and is gone, but it was only 9% of the neighbourhood
cost. The rest is one function below it --- axisSteps rescans its whole
candidate list per candidate. Skipping that scan where it cannot fire measured
12 MB / 2.24 ms on the same benchmark, 67% under baseline. Filed as
sized-grid-knm with the experiment and the class-contract question it raises.

This closes out the fold defect the IsCoordList note describes: all three
instances (AffineCoordList, npOffset, npStepsWithin) are now class methods.
close_reason: Closed

title: aoc 2018/11: squareSum rebuilds its corners list per position, 90,000 times a solve
description:
Found while re-pricing sized-grid-up6 against the real consumer.

src/2018/11.hs:

    squareSum size p sat =
      sum [s * index sat (p .+^ off) | (off, s) <- corners]
      where
        d = size - 1
        corners = [ (coordFromTuple (d, d), 1), ... ]

'corners' depends only on 'size', but it is bound inside squareSum, which is
called once per position -- 90,000 times per solve, 17 solves. So four Coords and
four tuples are built and thrown away per position.

MEASURED (scratch package, code copied unchanged, against the czf branch):

  solve 3, as written        8.02 ms
  solve 3, corners hoisted   4.12 ms

Hoisting halves the solve. Across 17 solves that is ~66 ms of a 207 ms program,
~31 percent -- comparable to what an unboxed Grid (sized-grid-up6) would buy on
the same program, and it is a one-line change in the consumer rather than a new
module in the library.

FIX: lift the comprehension into solve, where 'size' is already in scope, so
corners is built once per solve instead of once per position. The hoisted version
benchmarked above is exactly that.

Worth knowing for the library too: after sized-grid-0tj and sized-grid-czf the
whole program allocates 1.07 GB, down from 2.91 GB, and this list is a large part
of what is left. The library's own offset path is now 53 bytes per 360,000
offsets.

title: offsetCoord folds the axis list with a helper that cannot unroll, like AffineSpace did
description:
Split out of sized-grid-czf, which fixed the same defect one function along.

czf moved the (.+^)/(.-.) fold into the AffineCoordList class and 360,000 offsets
through a two-axis Coord went from 28.5 ms / 126 MB to 2.02 ms / 53 B. offsetCoord
(src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs) still has the old shape:

    offsetCoord (Coord cs) (Coord d) = Coord <$> helper cs d
      where
        helper :: (IsCoordList xs, AllDiffSame Int xs)
               => NP I xs -> NP I (MapDiff xs) -> Maybe (NP I xs)
        helper Nil Nil = Just Nil
        helper (I x :* xs) (I dx :* dxs) =
            (\\y ys -> I y :* ys) <$> offsetIsCoord x dx <*> helper xs dxs

Self-recursive and polymorphic in the axis list, so it cannot unroll, and every
axis after the first peels the dictionary at run time.

EVIDENCE it is worth doing. 'extend neighbourSum 50x50' did not move across czf:
9.17 ms / 28 MB before and after. That is 2,500 cells x 8 Moore neighbours =
20,000 offsets, i.e. ~1.4 KB per offset, against the 0 bytes an offset now costs
through (.+^). The neighbourhood path is what gameOfLife, ising-example and
../aoc/src/2015/18.hs and 2018/18.hs actually run.

APPROACH. Unlike czf this is NOT a new class and NOT a breaking change: the
per-axis step is offsetIsCoord, which needs IsCoordLifted x, and that is exactly
what IsCoordList already supplies per axis. So it is a new IsCoordList method:

    npOffset :: AllDiffSame Int cs => NP I cs -> NP I (MapDiff cs) -> Maybe (NP I cs)

AllDiffSame is a type family that reduces to equality constraints at a concrete
list, so it costs nothing at run time. Check that claim in the Core rather than
assuming it -- the whole point of czf was that the method signature must not
carry a constraint that has to be peeled per axis.

The same treatment probably applies to offsetCoordUpTo and coordRay, which walk
offsetCoord in a loop. Measure before extending the scope.

VERIFY WITH 'extend neighbourSum 50x50' in bench/Main.hs, following the
before/after procedure in that file's header. Do not read against the recorded CSV.
notes:
DONE. npOffset is an IsCoordList method; offsetCoord is now `Coord <$> npOffset cs d`.
MapDiff and AllDiffSame moved to SizedGrid.Coord.Class so the method can be stated
there. Purely additive to the public API: both were already re-exported from
SizedGrid.Coord under the same names, and nothing outside Coord.hs named either,
including ../aoc.

THE CORE CLAIM CHECKED, as the issue asked. At '[Clamped 300, Clamped 300] the fold
unrolls to two direct offsetIsCoord calls with no axis-list dictionary, and
`AllDiffSame Int cs` on the method signature costs nothing --- no evidence is passed
for it at all. The type family reduces to one `Diff x ~ Int` per axis and the

title: windowFits is an asserted axiom; try ghc-typelits-presburger to discharge it
description:
`SizedGrid.Internal.Type.windowFits` is the only `unsafeCoerce` in the library:

    windowFits :: forall n y z. Dict (n <= y, z <= (y - n))
    windowFits = unsafeCoerce (Dict :: Dict (0 <= 0, 0 <= 0))

It supplies the two facts `shrinkGrid` needs to call `dropGrid` then `takeGrid`.
Soundness rests entirely on the `x + z <= y + 1` constraint on the
`ShrinkableGrid` instance, which is checked at every call site -- so the axiom is
believed true, but it is asserted rather than derived, and an `unsafeCoerce`
producing a `Dict` is the single place where a mistake in that reasoning would
be silent.

The module comment already names the candidate fix and nobody has tried it:

> That wanted is a `<=` goal from `<=` givens over a truncating subtraction,
> which needs ghc-typelits-presburger; it stays an asserted axiom.

This is a bounded spike, not a redesign. Add `ghc-typelits-presburger` to the
`common lang` plugin list next to `natnormalise` and `knownnat`, delete
`windowFits`, and see whether the `shrinkGrid` call site still compiles.

Two acceptable outcomes, and both are worth having:

- It works: the library's last asserted axiom goes away, and
  `SizedGrid.Internal.Type` shrinks to just `requiring`.
- It does not: the comment gets upgraded from "needs presburger" (a guess) to a
  record of what was actually tried and how it failed, so the next reader does
  not re-run this spike.

Note the constraint that sank sized-grid-h56 applies here too: `-fplugin` is not
transitive. A plugin enabled for this library says nothing about a downstream
consumer. That is fine for `windowFits` specifically, because the goal is solved
*inside* this library at the `shrinkGrid` definition rather than being re-emitted
into a consumer's context -- but confirm that before concluding, because it is
exactly the assumption that made h56 look like a fix when it was not.
design:
The arithmetic the axiom stands in for, from the module comment:

At the use site the window offset `n` comes from `reifyCoord` on a coord of size
`x`, so `n + 1 <= x`, and the `ShrinkableGrid` instance requires
`x + z <= y + 1`. Together:

    n + 1 + z <= x + z <= y + 1        so   n + z <= y

which gives both `n <= y` (drop stays in range) and `z <= y - n` (the window fits
in what is left).

The first conjunct is ordinary linear arithmetic. The second mentions `y - n`,
GHC's *truncating* subtraction on Nat, over an existential `n` -- that is what
natnormalise will not do. Presburger arithmetic can express truncating
subtraction by case analysis on `n <= y`, and here the `n <= y` case is exactly
what the first conjunct establishes, which is the reason to expect this to work.

Verify rather than assume: check that ghc-typelits-presburger's current release
supports GHC 9.10/9.12/9.14 before adding it, since its GHC support has
historically lagged. If it only covers part of the tested-with range that is a
reason to reject, and should be recorded as such.
acceptance_criteria: Either windowFits is deleted and SizedGrid.Internal.Type exports only 'requiring', with the full test suite green on the tested-with GHCs; or the module comment records the concrete presburger attempt and why it failed, so the spike is not repeated.
close_reason:
Done, but not the way the issue predicted -- no plugin was added.

Presburger was tried first and it DOES discharge the goal: commit ae643ea has the
working change, all suites green on 9.12.3. It was rejected on the criterion this
issue's own design section set out. ghc-typelits-presburger 0.7.4.2 is bounded
'ghc <9.13', as is the ghc-tcplugins-extra 0.5 beneath it, with no 9.14 branch
upstream (last release supports 9.12). With it in build-depends GHC 9.14.1 fails
to resolve outright, [Cabal-7107] -- verified against a real 9.14.1 compiler, and
verified that removing that one dependency is what makes 9.14 resolve again. That
is precisely the trap that left h56 deferred; natnormalise and knownnat escaped it
by moving to ghc-tcplugin-api, and presburger has not moved.

The axiom turned out not to need a solver at all (commit 7bf7531). Probing
natnormalise showed the real limitation is broader than the issue assumed: it is
not just the truncating subtraction, it will not chain two '<=' givens at all and
fails on a bare 'a <= b, b <= c => a <= c'. But it does cancel constants from both
sides. So:

  - 'sliceGrid off len' replaces 'takeGrid len . dropGrid off', stating the bound
    as 'off + len <= m' rather than 'len <= m - off'. The truncating subtraction
    never appears. It is also V.slice's own precondition, so that bounds check
    cannot fire. Same elements: [off, off+len).
  - 'windowFits' keeps its name but is derived, not asserted, from plusMonotone1
    and leTrans in Data.Constraint.Nat. 'constraints' was already a dependency.

Net result: no unsafeCoerce in src/, no new dependency, GHC 9.14 kept.

Honest limit on the claim: plusMonotone1 and leTrans are themselves unsafeCoerce
inside 'constraints'. What changed is that the reasoning is machine-checked --
those are general lemmas about + and <=, where windowFits was a bespoke
three-variable claim about this library's window invariant, asserted whole. GHC
now verifies the composition yields 'n + z <= y' from the givens.

Verified on GHC 9.12.3 with -fforce-recomp: library, three examples and benchmarks
warning-free; 315 tasty tests, readme suite and the plugin-free downstream suite
all pass. The downstream suite passing is what shows the goal is solved at the
definition rather than re-emitted into a consumer's context.

Filed sized-grid-ior: tests/Main.hs and README.lhs have 8 pre-existing warnings
that only show on a cold build (confirmed present at c697f1b, so not from this
work).

'sliceGrid' is exported from SizedGrid.Internal.Grid but NOT added to the public
SizedGrid.Grid.Grid list -- deliberately left out of scope; worth deciding
separately, since dropGrid and takeGrid are both public and this is the more
useful primitive.

description:
sized-grid-k6n removed the constraint leak at the source. The five downstream signatures that were written around it can now lose it, but they are in ../aoc and were not touched by that change, so they still say it:

    ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:32  parse  :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => ...
    ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs:31  parse  :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => ...
    ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs:48  parser :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => ...
    ../aoc/src/2017/19.hs:35  parse  :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => ...
    ../aoc/src/2018/18.hs:36  parse  :: (KnownNat n, 1 <= n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => ...

title: Replace the AllGridSizeKnown type family with a class, so callers stop writing KnownNat (n * n)
description:
AllGridSizeKnown is a type family, so it emits 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize ...)' goals
at the call site instead of solving them. That is what makes puzzle code in ../aoc
write type-level arithmetic by hand:

    ../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:33
    parse :: (KnownNat n, KnownNat (n GHC.* n)) => String -> Maybe (Grid '[Clamped n, Clamped n] Cell)

'gridFromList' asks for 'AllGridSizeKnown cs' (src/SizedGrid/Internal/Grid.hs:253).
Being a *family* (Internal/Grid.hs:213-219) it expands to a conjunction --

    AllGridSizeKnown cs = ( KnownNat (CoordNat (Head cs))
                          , KnownNat (MaxCoordSize (Tail cs))
                          , KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)
                          , AllGridSizeKnown (Tail cs) )

-- and then does no solving at all: the raw 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)' goal lands
on the caller. For cs ~ '[Clamped n, Clamped n] that is 'KnownNat (n * (n * 1))',
which GHC cannot get from 'KnownNat n', so the caller states it by hand.

Contrast the AllSizedKnown *class* (src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:783-791): its instances
derive 'KnownNat (MaxCoordSize cs)' inductively from the per-axis KnownNats, so a
caller with 'KnownNat n' needs nothing else. Same obligation, discharged by
instance resolution rather than dumped on the caller.

Proposed: give the structural-recursion classes the same treatment -- replace the
AllGridSizeKnown family with a class carrying the evidence it currently demands
(gridFromList, collapseGrid, and the ToJSON/FromJSON instances at
Internal/Grid.hs:265,283 are the users), so the induction happens during instance
resolution.

Expected: '../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:33' loses 'KnownNat (n GHC.* n)' and reads
'parse :: KnownNat n => ...'.

WHY THIS AND NOT sized-grid-h56: h56 predicted the plugins would fix this. They
cannot -- type-checker plugins are not transitive. sized-grid enabling them affects
only sized-grid's own modules; ../aoc solves its own constraints and does not enable
them (verified: no 'typelits' in aoc.cabal, cabal.project or flake.nix). So this
leak is fixable only by an API change, and needs no plugin.
close_reason: Closed

title: asOrdinal is IsCoord's only required method and its Iso laws are untested
description:
Found 2026-08-12 while working out whether Test.Utils.isCoordLaws should be rewritten as properties (see sized-grid-05b).

IsCoord has exactly one required method, and its haddock states the obligation outright:

    -- | As each coord represents a finite number of states, it must be
    --   isomorphic to an Ordinal
    class IsCoord (c :: Nat -> Type) where
      asOrdinal :: Iso' (c n) (Ordinal n)
      (src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:50-53)

Everything else in the class is derivable from it. So 'asOrdinal is an isomorphism' is the load-bearing law of the whole coordinate abstraction -- and nothing checks it.

WHAT COVERAGE ACTUALLY EXISTS. Across the entire suite 'asOrdinal' appears three times:

    tests/Test/Utils.hs:361   view asOrdinal (zeroPosition @c @n)   -- one fixed value
    tests/Test/Utils.hs:368   view (asOrdinal @c) (maxCoord :: c n) -- one fixed value
    tests/Test/Ordinal.hs:114 view (re asOrdinal) (toEnum 3)        -- one fixed value

Three ground facts about three distinguished values. The round trip is never exercised at an arbitrary coord in either direction.

THE MISSING LAWS, which are the standard Iso laws:

    view asOrdinal . review asOrdinal == id     -- on Ordinal n
    review asOrdinal . view asOrdinal == id     -- on c n

for arbitrary values, over Periodic, Clamped and Ordinal. An 'Iso' that is not one is precisely the failure that produces silently wrong reads rather than errors: every index, tabulate and neighbour calculation goes through this conversion, so a coord type whose two directions disagree corrupts results everywhere without ever throwing.

Worth stating alongside them, since they are the same obligation seen from other angles:

    ordinalToNum (view asOrdinal c) is in [0, CoordNat c)     -- the range half
    reifyCoord c (\m -> natVal (Proxy @m)) == ordinalToNum (view asOrdinal c)

The second is partially covered already -- Test.Ordinal checks it at every value of an Ordinal 5 and at one Periodic 5 -- but it is written as examples rather than as a law over arbitrary coords.

WHY IT WAS MISSED: isCoordLaws is an HUnit testCase asserting facts about zeroPosition and maxCoord. Those are single values, so there was nothing to quantify over and the shape of the test never invited the question 'what varies here'. Rewriting it as properties is what surfaced the gap.
close_reason:
Added the missing quantified laws.

Test.Utils gains 'isoLaws', a generic bundle for any AnIso' -- both round trips,
labelled from the iso's name. isCoordLaws is now a testGroup: the three original
HUnit assertions (kept, as 'distinguished values' -- zeroPosition and maxCoord
are single values with nothing to quantify over) plus isoLaws on asOrdinal, the
range property, and reifyCoord-agrees-with-asOrdinal quantified over the coord.

Main.hs gains 'Ordinal 10' as an isCoordLaws call site -- it had none, and it is
the instance that overrides asOrdinal, zeroPosition, maxCoord and reifyCoord all
at once. isoLaws also picks up _WrappedCoord, the library's other exported Iso'.

315 -> 330 tests; downstream and readme suites still pass; no new warnings.

WHAT THE MUTATION TESTING ESTABLISHED, which is the part worth carrying forward:
only two of these four properties can actually fail.

  review asOrdinal . view asOrdinal == id   HAS TEETH. A non-injective instance
                                            (extra field dropped on the way out,
                                            invented on the way back) falsifies
                                            it within a handful of cases.
  reifyCoord agrees with asOrdinal          HAS TEETH. Verified with an
                                            off-by-one reifyCoord override; also
                                            caught by 'distinguished values'.
  view asOrdinal . review asOrdinal == id   CANNOT FAIL.
  asOrdinal lands in [0, n)                 CANNOT FAIL.

The last two are unfalsifiable because asOrdinal carries no KnownNat n, so an
instance cannot build an Ordinal n at all -- unsafeOrdinal and numToOrdinal both
need the size -- and the only ordinal it can return is the one it was handed.
They are the law written down, not tests, and they become real only if asOrdinal
ever gains that constraint. Recorded in memory so nobody adds more round-trip
properties expecting them to catch something.

DISCOVERED: sized-grid-6os. The range property quantifies over 'arbitrary',
which draws in-range by construction, so a coord built out of range by an
OPERATION is not reached -- and unsafeOrdinal's assert does not catch it either,
because cabal builds the suite at -O1 where assertions are compiled away.

title: Adopt quickcheck-classes and express our own laws in its Laws shape
description:
Investigated 2026-08-12 while closing sized-grid-ryy, which asked whether the hand-rolled law helpers in Test.Utils should lean on quickcheck-classes instead.

THE HEADLINE: quickcheck-classes does NOT provide the three law groups ryy added. Verified by grepping the 0.6.5.0 source rather than from memory -- its full law list is altLaws alternativeLaws applicativeLaws applyLaws bifoldableLaws bifunctorLaws bitraversableLaws bitsLaws boundedEnumLaws categoryLaws commutativeCategoryLaws commutativeMonoidLaws commutativeSemigroupLaws commutativeSemigroupoidLaws contravariantLaws enumLaws eqLaws euclideanLaws exponentialSemigroupLaws extendedPlusLaws foldableLaws functorLaws gcdDomainLaws genericLaws idempotentSemigroupLaws integralLaws isListLaws ixLaws jsonLaws monadLaws monadPlusLaws monadZipLaws monoidLaws muvectorLaws numLaws ordLaws plusLaws primLaws rectangularBandSemigroupLaws ringLaws semigroupLaws semigroupMonoidLaws semigroupoidLaws semiringLaws showLaws showReadLaws storableLaws substitutiveEqLaws traversableLaws.

No Comonad, no Representable, no Distributive. The only match for 'distributiv' in the whole package is Alt's left-distributivity, which is unrelated. So adopting it would not have saved any of the ryy work, and it does not replace Test.Utils.comonadLaws, representableLaws or distributiveLaws.

WHAT IT DOES COVER IS A REAL GAP. Grid has Functor, Applicative, Monad, Foldable and Traversable instances. The suite tests exactly one of those (Applicative, hand-rolled). Everything else is untested.

PROTOTYPED, NOT THEORISED. A scratch Test.Classes module wired into the tasty suite:

    lawsToTest :: Laws -> TestTree
    lawsToTest (Laws name props) = testGroup name (map (uncurry testProperty) props)

    classesTests = testGroup "quickcheck-classes on Grid" (map lawsToTest
      [ functorLaws     (Proxy @(Grid '[Periodic 3, Periodic 4]))
      , applicativeLaws (Proxy @(Grid '[Periodic 3, Periodic 4]))
      , monadLaws       (Proxy @(Grid '[Periodic 3, Periodic 4]))
      , foldableLaws    (Proxy @(Grid '[Periodic 3, Periodic 4]))
      , traversableLaws (Proxy @(Grid '[Periodic 3, Periodic 4]))
      ])

It compiled first try and added 32 passing laws -- Functor 3, Applicative 5, Monad 5, Foldable 11, Traversable 4 -- taking the suite from 315 to 347 tests with the total runtime unchanged at about 0.2s. Foldable is the biggest single win: 11 laws over fold, foldMap, foldr, foldr', foldl, foldl', foldl1, foldr1, toList, null and length, none of which is checked today.

CONSTRAINT FIT WAS THE THING I EXPECTED TO BLOCK IT, AND IT DOES NOT. On GHC over 8.5 the unary laws take quantified constraints (forall a. Arbitrary a => Arbitrary (f a), and the same for Eq and Show) rather than Arbitrary1/Eq1/Show1. Those discharge from the existing instances at a concrete cs with no new machinery, because AllSizedKnown is resolved there.

COST. On the 9.12 dev environment the solver needed three new builds: quickcheck-classes, quickcheck-classes-base and primitive-addr. Its aeson, vector, semirings and semigroupoids flags are all manual with default True, so they can be switched off with a constraints line if the dependency tree matters.

COMPATIBILITY. Solves on both GHC 9.12.3 and GHC 9.14.1, checked with cabal build --dry-run --enable-tests -w ghc-9.14.1. NOT verified to actually compile under 9.14 -- that needs a full rebuild of the dependency tree and is better answered by CI, see sized-grid-rt9. Base bound is base less than 5, so there is no bounds-level risk.
design:
THE 'IS IT TOO OLD' QUESTION, WITH DATES.

  - quickcheck-classes 0.6.5.0, uploaded 2021-04-12 by andrewthad. Not deprecated.
    Five years without a release.
  - hedgehog-classes 0.2.5.4, uploaded 2022-12-17 by chessai, revised 2025-06-03.
    It DOES have comonadLaws -- the only one of our three anyone ships -- but no
    Representable and no Distributive either. Adopting it means running Hedgehog
    alongside QuickCheck in one suite to buy a law group we now already have.
    Rejected on that trade.
  - checkers 0.6.0, uploaded 2022-03-08 by Conal Elliott with sjakobi, revised
    2023-03-13. Introduces its own EqProp and Model classes, which is precisely
    the buy-in quickcheck-classes advertises avoiding. Rejected.
  - No actively-released successor found. The whole niche is 2021-2022 vintage;
    there is no modern replacement to wait for.

CONCLUSION: 'old' here is release cadence, not breakage. The package has loose
bounds (base < 5), a small CPP-guarded implementation, and it solves on the
newest GHC this package targets. It is QuickCheck-native, so adoption is
additive rather than a framework switch, and the Laws-to-TestTree adapter is two
lines -- if it ever does break on a future GHC, dropping it costs one module and
the laws it was covering, not a rewrite of the suite.

RECOMMENDATION: adopt for the base classes, keep Test.Utils for the rest. The two
are complements, not alternatives. Test.Utils keeps what has no upstream at all:
comonadLaws, representableLaws and distributiveLaws (nobody ships the last two),
additiveGroupLaws and affineSpaceLaws (vector-space), traversalLaws (lens) and
isCoordLaws (library-specific).
notes:
2026-08-13 (from sized-grid-6p4): Test.Utils now has 'isoLaws :: String -> AnIso' s a -> TestTree', written deliberately WITHOUT quickcheck-classes. It is already in the Laws shape -- a name plus a list of named properties -- so converting it when this issue lands is mechanical.

Two facts for this issue to weigh:
  - quickcheck-classes ships no iso bundle, so isoLaws is ours either way. The
    package's value here is its bundles for the standard classes, which is what
    Test.Utils currently hand-rolls: semigroupLaws, monoidLaws, applicativeLaws,
    eq1Laws, distributiveLaws, comonadLaws.
  - it is NOT in the nix package set as it stands. 'ghc-pkg list' shows only
    QuickCheck-2.15.0.1 and tasty-quickcheck-0.11.1, so adopting it means
    touching flake.nix, not just the cabal file.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
EXTENDING WITH OUR OWN LAWS: prototyped 2026-08-12, and it works. This is the better plan than treating quickcheck-classes as a fixed menu.

The library's own idiom, straight from its README, is 'myLaws :: Proxy a -> [Laws]' -- a LIST of Laws per type. Laws is an ordinary exported record:

    data Laws = Laws { lawsTypeclass :: String, lawsProperties :: [(String, Property)] }

so our own law groups can be values of it and sit in that same list. Prototyped Comonad, Representable and Distributive in that shape alongside upstream's Functor/Applicative/Monad/Foldable/Traversable: 354 tests, all passing, 0.23s, and in the output nothing distinguishes ours from theirs --

      Grid
        Functor ... Foldable ... Traversable      (upstream)
        Representable
          tabulate . index == id:            OK   (ours)
        Distributive
          distribute . distribute == id:     OK   (ours)
      FocusedGrid
        Comonad
          extract . duplicate == id:         OK   (ours)

One 'lawsToTest :: Laws -> TestTree' adapter, two lines, renders both.

WHAT THE CONVERSION COSTS -- it is a rewrite of the helpers, not a wrapper:

  - The shape changes from 'proxy (w a)' to 'Proxy w', with the element type
    fixed internally (upstream uses Integer). That is what lets our laws join the
    same list as functorLaws, and it drops a Proxy argument, so it is an
    improvement rather than a concession.
  - Constraints change from saturated 'Arbitrary (w a)' to quantified
    'forall a. Arbitrary a => Arbitrary (w a)', matching upstream on GHC over 8.5.
    These discharge from our existing instances at a concrete cs. Even the
    coassociativity law, which needs Show (w (w (w a))) three levels deep,
    resolves through the quantified constraint -- that was the part I expected to
    fail and it does not.
  - QuantifiedConstraints is NOT implied by GHC2024, so the tests stanza needs it
    added to default-extensions. One line.

WHAT DOES NOT FIT. Laws holds [(String, Property)], so the two HUnit-based helpers
-- eq1Laws and isCoordLaws, both testCase rather than testProperty -- cannot become
Laws without being rewritten as properties. They can either be converted (their
assertEqual calls map onto (===) readably) or simply stay outside as plain
TestTrees. Also lost: per-property tasty options, since options can only be applied
to a whole rendered group. Neither is a real obstacle.

WHY THIS ANSWERS THE COUPLING WORRY. My earlier note said adopting quickcheck-classes
is safe because dropping it costs one module. Building OUR laws on its Laws type
looks like it undermines that -- if the package dies, our own laws die with it. It
does not, because Laws is a three-line record with no behaviour. If the package ever
breaks on a future GHC we define that record ourselves and lose only the BORROWED
laws; ours keep working untouched. The coupling is nominal, not structural.

BONUS: nobody ships Representable or Distributive laws anywhere in the ecosystem. In
this shape ours are directly upstreamable -- a PR to quickcheck-classes, or a small
package of its own.

comments.author: Kevin Horlick
comments.text:
ON REWRITING eq1Laws AND isCoordLaws AS PROPERTIES -- yes, but the reason matters, and a mechanical conversion would be a regression.

Look at what the two actually assert:

  eq1Laws     liftEq (==) (pure ()) (pure ()) is True.
              One ground fact. 'pure ()' is a single fixed value at a ~ (), so
              nothing varies.
  isCoordLaws three facts about zeroPosition and maxCoord, both single
              distinguished values.

As properties these re-run identical checks 100 times each: same coverage, 100x the work. If the only goal is fitting the Laws shape, QuickCheck's 'once' does that honestly -- 'property (once (x === y))' is one run, fits Laws, no waste.

The real improvement is that ATTEMPTING the conversion forces the question 'what varies here', and the answer turns out to be laws that do not exist yet:

  - asOrdinal is an Iso and its round trips are untested at arbitrary values. It
    is IsCoord's only required method, so it is the load-bearing law of the whole
    coordinate abstraction. Filed as sized-grid-6p4.
  - eq1Laws' law with content is 'liftEq (==) x y === (x == y)' over arbitrary
    x and y, not 'pure () == pure ()'.

So: convert, but convert by adding quantification where something genuinely varies. The zeroPosition and maxCoord facts should stay one-shot -- wrapped in 'once' if they need to live in a Laws value. Properties are not better than testCases per se; quantifying over a single inhabitant is just a slower testCase.

comments.text:
ON FORKING quickcheck-classes -- recommend against, and the alternative is strictly better shaped for the need.

WHAT A FORK OBLIGES YOU TO OWN. quickcheck-classes carries about 50 law groups, a six-flag matrix (aeson, vector, semirings, semigroupoids, unary-laws, binary-laws), CPP branches reaching back to GHC 7.4, and dependencies on primitive, primitive-addr and semirings. A fork means owning compatibility for all of that on every new GHC -- to gain three law groups that are roughly 100 lines.

A FORK IS ALSO THE WRONG SHAPE. Nothing in quickcheck-classes needs CHANGING. What is missing is purely additive: Comonad, Representable, Distributive. A fork implies divergence and rebasing forever; an additive package implies neither.

ORDER OF OPERATIONS. sized-grid cannot publish under its own name yet -- sized-grid-85n is still open and still P1. The cabal file names ed@wastell.co.uk as maintainer, edwardwas as author, and github.com/edwardwas/sized-grid as homepage, and the 'sized-grid' name on Hackage belongs to upstream. Taking on a SECOND package's maintenance before this one has an identity is out of order.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, in increasing order of commitment:

  (a) NOW: keep the laws in this suite. Zero overhead, and they are already written.
  (b) IF THEY EARN IT: publish a small additive package on top of
      quickcheck-classes-base, whose dependencies on a modern GHC are only base,
      QuickCheck, transformers and containers -- everything but QuickCheck is a
      boot library. Depend on it purely for the Laws type and contribute only
      what is missing. No fork, no divergence, no inherited compat burden, and it
      composes with quickcheck-classes for anyone using both. The ecosystem
      argument is real: Representable and Distributive laws are shipped by
      nobody, and hedgehog-classes is the only place comonadLaws exists at all.
  (c) PR UPSTREAM: worth one attempt, but temper expectations. The repo currently
      shows 17 open issues and 4 open pull requests, so PRs demonstrably sit. Do
      not block on it.

THE ONE CASE THAT WOULD JUSTIFY A FORK is quickcheck-classes actually breaking on a GHC this package needs, with upstream unresponsive. That is not the situation: it solves on 9.14.1 today. And if it ever happens, the Laws record is three lines with no behaviour, so the answer is to vendor that type, not to fork the package.

title: Apply the ray rewrite to ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs when sized-grid-dr1 reaches master
description:
sized-grid-dr1 added `coordRay` and `offsetCoordUpTo`, the offset that reports where
it hit the edge. ../aoc/src/2024/04.hs is the call site that asked for them and can
now drop the workaround it was built on.

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE ISSUE, AND WHEN TO DO IT

Exactly as sized-grid-bij: aoc/cabal.project lists ../sized-grid as a source package,
so aoc builds against the MAIN sized-grid checkout on master, not against any
.claude/worktrees branch. aoc keeps working while dr1 sits on branch
worktree-offset-boundary-report and this patch would not even compile until it lands.
Apply WITH the master merge, not before it.

aoc's working tree also has substantial uncommitted changes, which is why this was
verified out-of-tree rather than applied. Rebase if 2024/04.hs has moved.

WHAT CHANGES, AND WHY THE GRID TYPE CHANGES WITH IT

The day is a bounded word search: XMAS must not wrap round an edge. The grid was
nevertheless `Grid '[Periodic n, Periodic n]`, and the boundedness was simulated ---
strengthen every coordinate into a grid one cell larger, walk there, and let
`weakenCoord` reject anything that landed in the pad. That is what forced
`strengthenCoord`/`weakenCoord`, `mapMaybe (traverse weakenCoord)` and the three
`Dict` entailments (`plusNat`, `leTrans`, `plusMonotone2`).

With a ray that stops at an edge, the simulation is unnecessary: the axes become
`Clamped`, which is what the pad was imitating, and part one becomes
`take 3 (coordRay c d)` with a pattern match that drops the directions without room.
Part two becomes `traverse (offsetCoord c . coordFromTuple)` over the four diagonals.
partTwo's signature loses `KnownNat (n + 1)` and `n <= n + 1`.

VERIFICATION ALREADY DONE (2026-08-12, against the worktree build)

Using the scratch-project workaround in memory `sized-grid-aoc-cannot-be-cabal-built`,
with the extra deps from `sized-grid-aoc-typecheck-extra-deps`:

  - type-checks against the dr1 worktree
  - the module's own documented examples still answer 18 and 9
  - old and new agree on ALL FOUR answers over 300 random 12x12 grids, so the
    rewrite is behaviour-preserving and the real input still answers 2532/1941

The full input (input/2024/04.txt) is NOT in the repo, so 2532/1941 could not be
produced directly. The random-grid equivalence above is the evidence in its place.

THE PATCH

Apply from the aoc repo root with `git apply`.

```diff
--- a/src/2024/04.hs
+++ b/src/2024/04.hs
@@ -17,24 +17,23 @@
 import Control.Comonad (extend, extract)
 import Control.Comonad.Store (experiment)
 import Control.Lens (view)
-import Data.AffineSpace ((.+^))
 import Data.Attoparsec.ByteString.Char8 (Parser, char, choice, endOfLine, many1, parseOnly, sepBy)
 import Data.Bool (bool)
 import Data.ByteString qualified as BS (readFile)
-import Data.Constraint (withDict, (\\))
-import Data.Constraint.Nat (leTrans, plusMonotone2, plusNat)
 import Data.Function (on)
 import Data.Functor.Compose (Compose (..))
 import Data.Functor.Product (Product (Pair))
-import Data.Maybe (fromJust, mapMaybe)
-import GHC.TypeNats (KnownNat, type (+), type (<=))
+import Data.Maybe (fromJust)
+import GHC.TypeNats (KnownNat, type (<=))
 import GHC.TypeNats qualified as GHC
-import SizedGrid (Grid, IsGrid (asFocusedGrid), Periodic, StrengthenCoord (strengthenCoord), WeakenCoord (weakenCoord), gridFromList)
-import SizedGrid.Coord (Coord, coordFromTuple)
+import SizedGrid (Clamped, Grid, IsGrid (asFocusedGrid), gridFromList)
+import SizedGrid.Coord (Coord, coordFromTuple, coordRay, offsetCoord)
 
 data Cell = X | M | A | S deriving (Eq, Show)
 
-type Input n = Grid '[Periodic n, Periodic n] Cell
+-- The word must not wrap round the edge of the puzzle, so the axes are Clamped:
+-- a walk off the end of one stops instead of coming back on the other side.
+type Input n = Grid '[Clamped n, Clamped n] Cell
 
 -- (2532,1941)
 main :: IO ()
@@ -60,24 +59,18 @@
 solve :: forall n. (1 <= n, KnownNat n) => Input n -> Int
 solve = sum . fmap occurences . extend (\s -> if extract s == X then experiment applyContext s else mempty) . view asFocusedGrid
   where
-    applyContext :: Coord '[Periodic n, Periodic n] -> Context (Coord '[Periodic n, Periodic n])
+    applyContext :: Coord '[Clamped n, Clamped n] -> Context (Coord '[Clamped n, Clamped n])
     applyContext c =
-      Compose $
-        mapMaybe
-          (traverse weakenCoord)
-          [ Three i j k
-          | dy <- [-1 .. 1],
-            dx <- [-1 .. 1],
-            (dy, dx) /= (0, 0),
-            let d = coordFromTuple (dy, dx),
-            let i, j, k :: Coord '[Periodic (n + 1), Periodic (n + 1)]
-                i = strengthenCoord c .+^ d
-                j = i .+^ d
-                k = j .+^ d
-          ]
-          \\ plusNat @n @1
-          \\ leTrans @1 @n @(n + 1)
-          \\ plusMonotone2 @n @0 @1
+      Compose
+        [ Three i j k
+        | dy <- [-1 .. 1],
+          dx <- [-1 .. 1],
+          (dy, dx) /= (0, 0),
+          -- Three steps that way, or nothing: the ray stops at the edge, so a
+          -- direction without room for a whole word yields fewer than three
+          -- cells and the pattern match drops it.
+          [i, j, k] <- [take 3 (coordRay c (coordFromTuple (dy, dx)))]
+        ]
 
     occurences :: Context Cell -> Int
     occurences = length . filter (== Three M A S) . getCompose
@@ -88,19 +81,17 @@
 
 -- >>> partTwo example
 -- 9
-partTwo :: forall n. (1 <= n, KnownNat n, KnownNat (n + 1), n <= n + 1) => Input n -> Int
+partTwo :: forall n. (1 <= n, KnownNat n) => Input n -> Int
 partTwo = sum . fmap (bool 0 1 . isXmas) . extend (\s -> if extract s == A then experiment applyContext s else Compose Nothing) . view asFocusedGrid
   where
-    applyContext :: Coord '[Periodic n, Periodic n] -> ContextTwo (Coord '[Periodic n, Periodic n])
-    applyContext c' =
-      withDict (plusNat @n @1) . withDict (plusMonotone2 @n @0 @1) $
-        withDict (leTrans @1 @n @(n + 1)) $
-          let c :: Coord '[Periodic (n + 1), Periodic (n + 1)] = strengthenCoord c'
-           in Compose $
-                traverse weakenCoord $
-                  Pair
-                    (Two (c .+^ coordFromTuple (-1, -1)) (c .+^ coordFromTuple (1, 1)))
-                    (Two (c .+^ coordFromTuple (-1, 1)) (c .+^ coordFromTuple (1, -1)))
+    applyContext :: Coord '[Clamped n, Clamped n] -> ContextTwo (Coord '[Clamped n, Clamped n])
+    applyContext c =
+      -- One diagonal step each way, and all four have to land on the grid.
+      Compose $
+        traverse (offsetCoord c . coordFromTuple) $
+          Pair
+            (Two (-1, -1) (1, 1))
+            (Two (-1, 1) (1, -1))
 
     isXmas :: ContextTwo Cell -> Bool
     isXmas (Compose (Just (Pair l r))) = on (&&) (`elem` [Two M S, Two S M]) l r
```

title: ../aoc 2025/04 calls moorePoints, removed in 0.3.0.0
description:
../aoc/src/2025/04.hs:62 does not compile against sized-grid 0.3.0.0:

    neighs = experiment (filter (/= coord) . nubOrd . moorePoints 1) g

    src/2025/04.hs:62:55: error: [GHC-88464]
        Variable not in scope:
          moorePoints :: t0 -> Coord [Clamped n, Clamped n] -> [Coord [Clamped n, Clamped n]]

'moorePoints' was REMOVED in the 0.3.0.0 neighbourhood replacement (see ChangeLog).
Removal rather than deprecation was deliberate: the behaviour changed under an
otherwise compatible signature.

This call site is the exact idiom the ChangeLog migration note predicts -- it
works around both of the old API's defects at once, including the centre
('filter (/= coord)') and the duplicates the clamping '(.+^)' produced
('nubOrd'). The replacement does neither.

MIGRATION

    neighs = experiment neighbours g

'neighbours' is the Moore neighbourhood at radius one, already excluding the
centre and already duplicate-free. Both the 'filter' and the 'nubOrd' go. Check
whether 'nubOrd' (Data.Containers.ListUtils) is still used elsewhere in the file;
if not, drop the import or -Wall will flag it.

DISCOVERED how: type-checking aoc during sized-grid-7d1 (HardWrap -> Clamped).
This is NOT caused by that rename -- the rename diff to this file is purely the
type name, and the error names 'moorePoints'. Note the error text shows
'Coord [Clamped n, Clamped n]' resolving correctly.

SIBLING of sized-grid-bb5, which covers the OTHER pre-existing aoc breakage
(the sealed-Grid reach-through at 2018/11.hs:31). aoc needs both before it builds.

CANNOT BE VERIFIED BY 'cabal build' in this environment: aoc depends on
hmatrix-0.20.2, whose configure step fails with 'Missing (or bad) C libraries:
blas, lapack'. Type-check individual modules instead -- see the
sized-grid-aoc-cannot-be-cabal-built memory for the exact recipe.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG

experiment f w = fmap (peek w) (f (pos w)), so the neighbourhood is centred on
'pos g', NOT on 'coord'. In forklift, 'pos g' is the parse-time focus (0,0) and
never moves, while 'coord' varies over every cell. So forklift inspected the
corner's neighbourhood for all 100 cells. On the example that region is
{(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)} holding 2 Paper, so 'papers < 4' was always True and
forklift was degenerately constant.

Sibling call sites confirm the intended idiom: 2015/18.hs:51 and 2018/18.hs:67

on. 2025/04 wrote 'filter (/= coord)' -- a mis-adaptation.

  B this issue's fix   solve=71  partTwo=71   <- identical to A, bug preserved
  C centred on coord   solve=13  partTwo=43   <- both match d050263's originals

  neighs = experiment neighbours (seek coord g)

title: Export the coordinate distance axisSteps already computes
description:
Inspiration: `Data.Manifold.Riemannian`'s `Geodesic` class, which asks a manifold for the
path between two points rather than leaving the caller to reconstruct it.

But the real point of this issue is smaller and cheaper than that: SIZED-GRID ALREADY
COMPUTES THE DISTANCE AND THEN THROWS IT AWAY.

    src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:398  axisSteps   :: IsCoordLifted x => Int -> x -> [(Int, x)]
    src/SizedGrid/Coord.hs:423  stepsWithin :: All IsCoordLifted cs
                                            => Int -> Coord cs -> [(Int, Coord cs)]

`axisSteps` computes the TRUE per-axis distance, and its own documentation
(Coord.hs:386-397) explains that this is the hard part:

    "Where two offsets reach the same value --- which a torus axis does as soon as
     2 * r >= n --- the one that took fewer steps wins, so the recorded distance is the
     true distance on that axis rather than whichever offset the enumeration happened to
     try first."

`stepsWithin` sums that across axes. And then both consumers discard the `Int`:

    mooreNeighbours      r c = [n | (s, n) <- stepsWithin r c, s > 0]           -- :454
    vonNeumannNeighbours r c = [n | (s, n) <- stepsWithin r c, s > 0, s <= r]   -- :471

Neither `axisSteps` nor `stepsWithin` is exported --- check the export list at
Coord.hs:6-39. So the library contains a correct, wrap-aware, mixed-boundary-policy
distance function that no caller can reach.

PROPOSAL

1. Export the distance directly. Both metrics fall out of the same per-axis numbers:

     coordDistance     :: All IsCoordLifted cs => Coord cs -> Coord cs -> Int  -- L-infinity
     coordManhattan    :: All IsCoordLifted cs => Coord cs -> Coord cs -> Int  -- L-1

   Note these must NOT be built on `stepsWithin`, which is radius-bounded and enumerates
   the whole neighbourhood --- that would be O(r^d) to answer a question that is O(d).
   Factor the per-axis "shorter route wins" rule out of `axisSteps` into a scalar
   `axisDistance :: IsCoordLifted x => x -> x -> Int` and build all three on it.

2. Export `stepsWithin` itself. It is the general primitive (every coord within radius r,
   paired with its true distance), both neighbourhood functions are one-liners over it,
   and BFS-shaped consumers want the distances.

WHY THIS IS THE CHEAPEST ITEM IN THE SET

The semantics are already written, reviewed and covered by the neighbourhood tests. The
work is factoring a scalar out of a list comprehension and adding names to an export
list. No type-level machinery, no breaking change --- purely additive.

CORRECTNESS NOTE

`coordDistance` on a mixed `'[HardWrap 5, Periodic 5]` coord must use each axis's own
policy: the bounded axis measures straight, the torus axis takes the shorter way round.
That is the behaviour `axisSteps` already has and is exactly what a caller cannot easily
write by hand, which is the argument for exporting it.
design: Factor the per-axis 'shorter route wins' rule out of axisSteps into a scalar axisDistance, then build coordDistance, coordManhattan and axisSteps on it. Do NOT implement distance via stepsWithin: that is radius-bounded and O(r^d) for an O(d) question.

    offset, ascending, so the centre sits in the middle'; enumerating values

    would break the 'a torus axis is ordered by offset, not by value' test.

title: Missing API: boundary detection (Interior/Boundary from manifolds)
description:
Inspiration: `SemimanifoldWithBoundary` in the `manifolds` package, which makes the
boundary a first-class part of the type rather than something callers rediscover:

    type Interior m; type Boundary m
    separateInterior :: m -> Either (Boundary m) (Interior m)

sized-grid has NO API for "is this coordinate on an edge". Not a predicate, not an
enumeration, nothing. Every consumer hand-rolls it against `natVal`:

    ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs:59-62
      n = fromEnum (natVal (Proxy @n)) - 1
      isCorner ((fromEnum -> r) :| (fromEnum -> c) :| _) =
        (r == 0 || r == n) && (c == 0 || c == n)

That is the whole of a boundary check written out per call site, and it is wrong the
moment an axis is `Periodic` --- a torus has no corners, but the code above will happily
report some.

PROPOSAL

Add a method to `IsCoord` (src/SizedGrid/Coord/Class.hs:32), following exactly the shape
`offsetIsCoord` established: a default that does the bounds check, which edgeless coord
types override.

    data Extremum = AtMin | AtMax deriving (Eq, Ord, Show, Enum, Bounded)

    -- in class IsCoord:
    coordBoundary :: (KnownNat n, 1 <= n) => c n -> Maybe Extremum
    coordBoundary c
      | i == 0                 = Just AtMin
      | i == ordinalSize @n - 1 = Just AtMax
      | otherwise              = Nothing
      where i = ordinalToInt (c ^. asOrdinal)

`Periodic` overrides it to `const Nothing`, for the same reason it overrides
`offsetIsCoord` to be total: a torus has no edges. That symmetry is the argument for
putting it in the class rather than writing a free function over `Coord`.

Then over a whole coord:

    coordBoundaries :: All IsCoordLifted cs => Coord cs -> NP (K (Maybe Extremum)) cs
    onBoundary      :: All IsCoordLifted cs => Coord cs -> Bool   -- any axis at an edge
    isCorner        :: All IsCoordLifted cs => Coord cs -> Bool   -- every axis at an edge

`isCorner` on an all-`Periodic` coord is then `False` by construction, which is the
correct answer and the one the hand-rolled version gets wrong.

RELATED, worth doing in the same change

`interiorCoords` / a `Grid` traversal restricted to cells whose full Moore neighbourhood
exists. Cellular automata want exactly this: ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs and gameOfLife both
special-case edge cells, and `mooreNeighbours` (Coord.hs:453) already returns a shorter
list at an edge without saying so.

ACCEPTANCE

../aoc/src/2015/18.hs can delete its `n`/`isCorner` local definitions and call the
library instead, and the result is still correct for `HardWrap` axes.
design: Add coordBoundary as an IsCoord method with a bounds-check default, mirroring exactly how offsetIsCoord is structured: bounded types take the default, Periodic overrides because a torus has no edges. That symmetry is why it belongs in the class rather than being a free function over Coord.
acceptance_criteria: ../aoc/src/2015/18.hs deletes its local n/isCorner definitions and calls the library; isCorner on an all-Periodic coord returns False.
notes:
CORRECTION to the note above, on the Grid traversal half.

The earlier note said the traversal 'does not serve the consumers cited' because an
extend-based automaton must produce a value for every cell. That reasoning is about the
CA pipeline and it stands, but it was the wrong answer to the question. The right answer
is that the traversal needs no new API at all:

    interior = itraversed . indices (not . onBoundary)
    boundary = itraversed . indices onBoundary

Grid cs is already TraversableWithIndex (Coord cs) (src/SizedGrid/Internal/Grid.hs:192),
so the index IS the coordinate and Control.Lens.indices does the filtering. Verified: on
a Clamped 5 x Clamped 5, lengthOf interior is 9, its indices are exactly interiorCoords,
'g & interior .~ 9' leaves all 16 boundary cells untouched, and 'indices isCorner' picks
out four cells. On a Periodic 5 x Periodic 5 the interior is all 25.

That composition is strictly better than what a named function would have given, because
it reads AND writes where interiorCoords only enumerates. Naming it would add a signature
and a second way to say the same thing and no capability, so it stays unnamed and is
documented on interiorCoords, in the README, and in the ChangeLog, with six tests in
tests/Test/Boundary.hs pinning it -- a documented composition nothing exercises is a
claim, not a fact.

So the 'RELATED, worth doing in the same change' half of this issue is now fully
addressed: interiorCoords for the enumeration, the optic for read-write, neither of them
requiring the consumer to know what natVal is.
